scenes.learnerAction: Use the model, complete its task, and explain what the representation shows.

content.body: This original informational passage explains an invented seed-library system. It gives definitions, procedures and reasons rather than telling a narrative. Keep the invented example separate from claims about real schools. Read the complete passage before answering.

accessibility.textAlternative: This original informational passage explains an invented seed-library system. It gives definitions, procedures and reasons rather than telling a narrative. Keep the invented example separate from claims about real schools. Read the complete passage before answering. How a seed library works. A seed library is a shared collection of seeds for planting. In this invented school example, families contribute in several ways. Some donate seeds; others clean storage tins or teach pupils when to plant. No family must pay money to take part. Pupils label each tin with the seed type and record each loan. The record helps the group know what is available. Borrowers return some seeds after their harvest so the collection can be used again. As a result, more pupils can borrow seeds in the next planting season. Dry storage helps protect the collection. Damp seeds may develop mould and become unsuitable for planting. Pupils inspect the tins each week and keep them in a dry cupboard. This example explains a possible system; it does not report measured results from a real school.

blocks.title: How a seed library works
paragraphs: A seed library is a shared collection of seeds for planting. In this invented school example, families contribute in several ways. Some donate seeds; others clean storage tins or teach pupils when to plant. No family must pay money to take part.

Pupils label each tin with the seed type and record each loan. The record helps the group know what is available. Borrowers return some seeds after their harvest so the collection can be used again. As a result, more pupils can borrow seeds in the next planting season.

Dry storage helps protect the collection. Damp seeds may develop mould and become unsuitable for planting. Pupils inspect the tins each week and keep them in a dry cupboard. This example explains a possible system; it does not report measured results from a real school.

sentences.why: Donating seeds, cleaning tins and teaching are explicitly named actions.

sentences.text: Pupils inspect the tins each week and keep them in a dry cupboard.
sentences.why: This describes pupil storage routines, not the different forms of family help.
